Motoring categories only. mileage : Vehicle mileage in miles. Motoring categories only. engineCc : Engine size in cc. Motoring categories only. batteryHealth : Battery percentage parsed from text, or null . storageGb : Storage in GB for single-capacity ads, or null . storageOptionsGb : Array of capacities mentioned in ad copy. isMultiVariant : True when one ad sells several capacities at several prices, so the tile price belongs to one unstated variant. matchedKeyword : Search keyword that matched this ad. Pro tips Ceiling awareness on deep pagination: Gumtree serves at most 50 pages per search (about 30 per page, capping results at about 1,500 ads per search). For large queries yielding thousands of ads, segment your sweep by specific location slugs like "london" or narrower price brackets. Promoted placements handling: Gumtree pins five promoted ads at the top of each page (measured on pages 1, 2, 3 and 5), regardless of sorting; the Actor flags Featured, Urgent and Spotlight labels as promoted. Set excludeFeatured: true if you wish to drop these promoted placements. Private versus Trade filtering: When auditing used vehicles, set sellerType: "private" to exclude Trade sellers, as Gumtree labels them, and focus exclusively on private sales. The Actor applies this filter after fetching, dropping Trade listings before dataset storage. Keyword match enforcement: requireKeywordMatch is enabled by default to drop irrelevant search matches where listing titles omit any word from your query. Start small with item caps: When developing automation pipelines, begin with maxItems: 20 to verify data mappings before running larger sweeps. If this happens, verify your search term spelling and ensure your price or location filters are not overly restrictive. Seller type returning null: Remember that sellerType is only published by Gumtree for motoring categories (such as "cars" ). Non-motoring categories do not publish seller classifications on listing cards. Handling invalid categories: category accepts one of 11 fixed slugs; for any other value the platform refuses the input before the run starts. Online dating platforms make it easier to connect with people, explore shared interests, and build relationships across geographic boundaries. Similarly, a photograph-based check does not necessarily establish a person's intentions or guarantee that the account will remain secure. It is useful to distinguish three concepts: Account verification: A platform-defined process that checks specific account information. Profile authenticity: The extent to which a profile accurately represents the person using it. Account security: The measures that help prevent unauthorized access, data exposure, and account takeover. These concepts overlap, but they are not interchangeable. How to Choose a Reliable Verification Resource The internet contains many websites that discuss verified accounts, identity checks, and dating profile security. Look for Clear Privacy Information A credible resource should explain what information it collects, why it needs that information, and how it handles personal data. Instead of treating the claims as proof, Sophie considers the possibility that the original owner could retain access or that the transfer could violate platform rules. She decides that using the platform's own account procedures is a more responsible approach. This case illustrates why account descriptions alone cannot establish security or legitimacy. Building Better Digital Habits Good account security is not a single action. It is a collection of habits that help users manage information, communicate responsibly, and respond to problems. Create a Simple Account Maintenance Routine Set aside time periodically to review account settings, check recovery information, update outdated profile details, and remove unnecessary permissions where supported. title: Make Unresolved Decisions Visible Before a Specification Reaches Engineering
author: Anuj Sadani
summary: A specification can look complete while containing two limits for the same field and an unanswered question about who may approve an action. A reviewer might notice both, but the next revision can make it hard to tell which findings were discussed and which still apply. Spec Sentry explores a narrow approach: annotate the facts that need mechanical checks, then keep review decisions in a separate ledger. This is most useful when a team is willing to make important uncertainty explicit. The checker does not promise to find every contradiction in ordinary prose. Declare the parts that must agree The fixture contains these declarations: @quantity preview.max_size = 10 MB @quantity preview.max_size = 10 GB @decision sharing-policy | pending | Who may invite guests? Both quantities use the same key but declare conflicting values or units. The pending decision makes an unanswered product question visible instead of leaving an engineer to invent a default. Term references can also be explicit: The initial preview uses [[term:external collaborator]]. @define workspace: A named product collaboration area. The undefined external collaborator reference becomes a finding. A definition for a different term does not resolve it. These directives use a small documented grammar. They are easy to inspect because they declare the thing being checked instead of asking the checker to infer the meaning of every sentence. Check the fixture Use Python 3.11 or newer. The runtime needs no third-party dependencies: git clone https://github.com/asadani/spec-sentry.git cd spec-sentry out_dir = " $( mktemp -d ) " python -m spec_sentry check sharing-spec.md \ --root fixtures --out " $out_dir /findings.json" The command exits with status 1 because the example intentionally contains findings. Status 0 means no configured findings were observed; status 2 indicates invalid input or an operational error. The output locates the conflicting declarations, undefined marked term, and pending decision. It gives the reviewer source evidence to inspect rather than editing the document. A reviewer decision belongs to a version A reviewer can accept, dismiss, or defer a finding with a note. The decision ledger is separate from the specification and records the fingerprint associated with the review. That separation matters after an edit. A dismissal against an older version should not automatically hide a finding in new text. When the relevant evidence changes, the prior disposition becomes stale and needs another look. The report excludes only fresh dismissed findings from its unresolved result. Accepting a finding records a review decision; it does not erase the underlying issue. This keeps discussion history distinct from a claim that the specification is now correct. The full walkthrough demonstrates the check, decision, and report lifecycle with a temporary copy of the fixture. Pay attention to the cost of annotations Explicit syntax trades broad coverage for reproducible checks. If a limit appears only in prose without a declared quantity, the tool cannot assume that it belongs to a matching key. Markdown headings do not create implicit scopes, and units are compared as written rather than converted. Those limits affect how a team should use the tool. Annotate the few quantities, terms, and decisions that repeatedly create ambiguity. Do not require a new notation for every sentence unless it produces enough useful findings to justify the authoring burden. The same principle applies to review ledgers. A ledger that requires more effort than it saves will become another stale artifact. Try it before a planning handoff Take one small feature spec with a few consequential limits and unresolved questions. Add the explicit declarations, run the check, and review the findings with the engineer who will implement the feature. Measure whether the check surfaces something actionable and whether the recorded decisions survive the next revision without concealing new uncertainty. That is a more useful test than counting annotations or declaring the document approved because the report is clean. The MIT-licensed repository includes the grammar, ledger format, fixtures, and checks. It offers a bounded way to keep selected questions visible through review. AI disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance using the project's implementation and synthetic specification. It does not report a measured reduction in specification defects.

title: Calling open models inside a TEE with the OpenAI Python SDK
author: VoltageGPU
summary: If you already call OpenAI from Python, switching to an open model that runs in a trusted execution environment (TEE) is two lines: the base URL and the key. Here is what that looks like, with real output captured on 23 October 2026. The two lines that change from openai import OpenAI import os client = OpenAI ( base_url = " https://api.voltagegpu.com/v1 " , api_key = os . environ [ " VOLTAGEGPU_API_KEY " ], # a vgpu_... key, never commit it ) resp = client . chat . completions . create ( model = " google/gemma-4-31B-turbo-TEE " , messages = [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : " In one sentence, what does a TEE protect? " }], ) print ( resp . choices [ 0 ]. message . content ) Every model id ends in -TEE : the model runs in an Intel TDX guest with confidential-computing NVIDIA GPUs. Streaming works as usual ( stream=True ). What came back x-voltagegpu-model: google/gemma-4-31B-turbo-TEE x-voltagegpu-confidential: tee x-voltagegpu-cost-usd: 0.000025 answer: A TEE protects sensitive data and code from being accessed or modified by the rest of the device's operating system. usage: 36 prompt + 25 completion tokens The response headers tell you which model actually ran and what the call cost, so you can log it next to your own usage. Listing the models GET /v1/models is public and returns, for each model, its live status (available, busy, saturated, unavailable), the price per million tokens and the context length. On 23 October there were 14 models, from small ones such as Mistral Nemo up to Qwen3.5-397B, DeepSeek V3.2 and Kimi K3. What the TEE does and does not give you GET /v1/attestation returns the Intel and NVIDIA evidence of the running instances, bound to a nonce you choose. It proves genuine TDX guests with confidential-computing GPUs. It does not prove which instance served a given response, nor which code runs inside. If you need to check the hardware evidence yourself, offline, the open-source voltage-verify verifies an Intel TDX quote and NVIDIA attestation tokens against a manifest you control. Same thing with LiteLLM, LangChain or LlamaIndex Because the API is OpenAI-compatible, the usual integrations work by pointing them at the base URL. Tested examples for each, with their unedited output, are in the cookbook: github.com/VoltageGPU/voltagegpu-cookbook . Disclosure: I build VoltageGPU.

title: Add persistent memory to a LlamaIndex agent (Memory, memory blocks and a retriever)
author: Mohammed Rafay
summary: Disclosure: I'm Mohammed, founder of MemorySync. I drafted this article with AI assistance and reviewed it for accuracy against the official MemorySync and LlamaIndex docs. The code is adapted from the docs and I haven't run it. LlamaIndex agents already have memory. Pass a Memory object to agent.run(..., memory=memory) and the agent gets a short-term chat buffer plus optional long-term "memory blocks". Two things surprise people when they try to make it remember a user across sessions: By default the Memory class uses an in-memory SQLite database, so the buffer is gone when the process restarts ( LlamaIndex memory docs ). Memory blocks only receive messages when the short-term buffer overflows. The defaults are token_limit=30000 and chat_history_token_ratio=0.7 , so nothing is flushed to long-term memory until the chat history passes about 21,000 tokens. Most real conversations never get that long. This post fixes both with MemorySync's LlamaIndex integration, llamaindex-memorysync . MemorySync is a hosted memory layer, and I'm building it. LlamaIndex behaviour comes from the official memory guide linked above. Everything about MemorySync comes from its LlamaIndex Memory guide . The code is adapted from those docs. I haven't run it for this post, so check it against your versions. What you'll set up A drop-in Memory that sends each user message for fact extraction as it arrives and recalls relevant facts on later runs, for the same user, in any thread. Optional: the recall block on its own, composed with blocks you already use. Optional: memories as a LlamaIndex retriever, a query engine or an agent tool. Optional: five memory tools and three helpers. Install pip install llamaindex-memorysync Per the guide it needs llama-index-core 0.13+ and Python 3.10+. PyPI currently lists 1.1.0 with llama-index-core>=0.13,<0.15 . Set MEMORYSYNC_API_KEY in the environment, or pass api_key , and keep it server-side. This is Python only. The guide points TypeScript users to the Vercel AI SDK or Mastra integrations. Step 1: Swap in MemorySyncMemory from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI from llamaindex_memorysync import MemorySyncMemory memory = MemorySyncMemory . from_defaults ( user_id = " customer-7 " , # required: scopes memory to one end user session_id = " thread-42 " , # groups the stored facts by thread ) agent = FunctionAgent ( tools = [...], llm = OpenAI ( model = " your-model " )) # First conversation await agent . run ( " I ' m vegetarian and I fly aisle. " , memory = memory ) # A later run for the same user response = await agent . run ( " Book my trip: flight plus a dinner spot. " , memory = memory ) MemorySyncMemory is a subclass of LlamaIndex's Memory , not a wrapper, so token_limit , insert_method and any extra blocks still work. What changes, per the guide: Each user message is sent to MemorySync when it's added to memory (on aput ), not when the buffer overflows. Short conversations persist too. Only user messages are sent. Assistant replies, system prompts and tool traffic stay in the short-term buffer. recall=False or persist=False turns either half off. The guide also spells out failure handling. The short-term buffer write happens first and its errors propagate. The MemorySync write comes after and reports through on_error instead of failing the turn. If recall fails, no memory block is rendered and the chat history still flows. Note that the short-term buffer is still LlamaIndex's own. If you also want the raw transcript to survive restarts, LlamaIndex's docs show passing async_database_uri (for example a Postgres URI) or your own chat_store to Memory.from_defaults . I'm assuming those pass through, since the guide says every standard Memory kwarg does, but I haven't tested it. Step 2: Who owns the memory user_id is the memory owner. Take it from your authenticated user record, not from the request body and not from a session id. A new user_id is a new, empty memory. session_id only groups facts by thread, so the same user gets the same memories in a new thread. Step 3 (optional): Compose the block yourself If you already run your own Memory with blocks like FactExtractionMemoryBlock or VectorMemoryBlock , add the recall block next to them: from llama_index.core.memory import Memory from llamaindex_memorysync import MemorySyncMemoryBlock memory = Memory . from_defaults ( session_id = " thread-42 " , memory_blocks = [ MemorySyncMemoryBlock ( user_id = " customer-7 " ), # ...alongside any other blocks you already run ], ) Recall renders into LlamaIndex's own memory template. Keep the flush rule in mind, though: in this setup the block only receives the user messages the buffer flushes into it. If you want every user message stored right away, use MemorySyncMemory from Step 1. The guide says a message sent on both paths is recognised server-side and extracted once. Truncation is the other difference. LlamaIndex's docs say that when blocks plus chat history exceed token_limit , blocks are truncated in priority order, and by default a truncated block is removed entirely. The guide says MemorySyncMemoryBlock drops its lowest-value lines instead, so the top memories stay in the prompt. Step 4 (optional): Memories as a retriever from llama_index.core.query_engine import RetrieverQueryEngine from llama_index.core.tools import RetrieverTool from llamaindex_memorysync import MemorySyncRetriever retriever = MemorySyncRetriever ( user_id = " customer-7 " , similarity_top_k = 5 ) nodes = retriever . retrieve ( " dietary preferences " ) # scored nodes engine = RetrieverQueryEngine . from_args ( retriever = retriever , llm = llm ) answer = engine . query ( " What do we know about this customer ' s diet? " ) tool = RetrieverTool . from_defaults ( retriever = retriever , name = " memory_search " , description = " Search everything known about this user. " , ) It's a standard BaseRetriever (sync and async), with the memory id and user in node metadata. similarity_top_k accepts 1 to 50. Unlike the memory classes, it raises on API failure instead of returning an empty list, so a RAG pipeline can tell "no memories" from "the service errored". Step 5 (optional): Tools and helpers from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent from llamaindex_memorysync import create_memorysync_tools agent = FunctionAgent ( tools = create_memorysync_tools ( user_id = " customer-7 " ), llm = llm , system_prompt = " Use the memory tools to remember durable facts. " , ) # For agents you don't fully trust: search and list only create_memorysync_tools ( user_id = " customer-7 " , read_only = True ) The tools are add_memory , search_memory , list_memories , update_memory (tags and importance only; memory text can't be changed) and delete_memory . They return readable error strings instead of raising. For code outside an agent, there are sync helpers: from llamaindex_memorysync import get_memory_context , save_turn , search_memories context = get_memory_context ( " what should I cook? " , user_id = " customer-7 " ) # "" for a new user hits = search_memories ( " dietary preferences " , user_id = " customer-7 " ) # Explicit persistence. This one raises on failure. save_turn ( user_id = " customer-7 " , user = " I ' m vegetarian " , assistant = " Noted! " , session_id = " thread-42 " ) save_turn sends only the user message. API errors raise MemorySyncAPIError , which carries the HTTP status and server detail. Troubleshooting Nothing is remembered after a short chat. You're probably using a plain block inside Memory , which only sees flushed messages. Switch to MemorySyncMemory . A new thread knows nothing. Check that user_id is identical in both runs. session_id can differ. The memory block disappears in long chats. That's LlamaIndex's default truncation for other blocks. Check their priority values; priority=0 blocks are always kept. Version errors. The package targets llama-index-core 0.13 to 0.14. Sources MemorySync LlamaIndex Memory guide: docs.memorysync.io/guides/llamaindex LlamaIndex memory guide: developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework/module_guides/deploying/agents/memory/ PyPI: llamaindex-memorysync 1.1.0 Try it If you want to see the save, reload and recall loop before wiring up an agent, the MemorySync playground runs it in your browser: memorysync.io/try .

title: New challenge: Build a gamer sign-up form
author: Matt Studdert
summary: We've launched a new free challenge: a gamer sign-up form. You'll build the sign-up screen for NEONCORE, a competitive-gaming network where players register as "operators" with a callsign. It's a junior-level project that helps you practice form validation, JavaScript-driven states, and accessible forms. What you'll build There's one form on the page, and every part of it has states to build: Four fields for a callsign, email, password, and password confirmation, plus a terms checkbox Validation messages that appear when a field loses focus, then update as the user fixes them Show and hide buttons for both password fields A password strength meter that updates from the first character A loading state on the submit button, followed by a success message that replaces the form A split layout on desktop that stacks on tablet and mobile What's included This is a free challenge, so the starter code gives you everything you need to build without a Figma file: Design screenshots for desktop and mobile, plus the error, filled, success, password strength, submitting, hover, and focus states A style guide with the colors, fonts, text presets, and spacing The fonts (Orbitron and JetBrains Mono), plus the logo and icons A starter HTML file with all the content written out, including every error message A README that explains how the form should behave between states, since a screenshot can't show that What you'll practice Validating fields on blur and re-checking them as the user types Writing clear, specific error messages and connecting them to their fields Moving focus and announcing changes to screen reader users Scoring password strength from length and character types Handling loading and success states without a server Building a dark, high-contrast interface that still meets WCAG AA How to start Head to the challenge page , download the starter code, and read through the README. It lists the user stories, explains when each field gets checked, and gives the password strength rules. From there, it's over to you. If AI tools are part of your workflow, lean on them to understand concepts and review your code, not to generate code. You'll learn far more by writing the validation logic yourself. Share your progress in our Discord community , ask for a review of your solution, and see how others handled the same states. We'd love to see what you build. title: Playwright و اسکرپ سایت‌های جاوااسکریپتی
author: Mohammad Zanjani
summary: اگر می‌پرسید اسکرپ با Playwright یعنی چه، پاسخ این است: وقتی دادهٔ عمومی فقط بعد از اجرای جاوااسکریپت در مرورگر دیده می‌شود، یک درخواست HTTP خام HTML خالی یا ناقص برمی‌گرداند و باید همان صفحه را در مرورگر واقعی رندر کرد. Playwright چارچوب اتوماسیون مرورگر است، نه میانبر دورزدن قفل. کارش خواندن DOM بعد از رندر است؛ جایگزین API رسمی و مجوز منبع نیست. پیشنهاد گوگل و جست‌وجوهای نزدیک معمولاً این نیت را دارند: «Playwright چیست»، «اسکرپ سایت جاوا اسکریپتی»، «تفاوت Playwright و Scrapy»، «تفاوت Playwright و Selenium»، «اسکرپ SPA»، «سلکتور پایدار» و «هزینه مرورگر هدلس». در این راهنما تعریف، زمان کافی‌نبودن HTML، مرز با Scrapy، پایداری سلکتور و هزینهٔ اجرا را می‌نویسیم. تعریف استخراج را در اسکرپ دیتا چیست ببینید، قرارداد دسترسی را در تفاوت اسکرپ و API ، و محدودهٔ مسئولانه را در وب اسکرپینگ قانونی است . اجرای پروژه‌های مجاز در خدمت اسکرپ داده روبینش است. Playwright is an open-source automation library for browser testing. Playwright can automate Chromium, Firefox and WebKit with a single API. Source: Playwright — Installation مرورگر وقتی لازم است که داده در HTML خام نیست. Playwright چیست و برای اسکرپ چه نقشی دارد؟ Playwright کتابخانه‌ای است که کرومیوم، فایرفاکس و وب‌کیت را از یک API کنترل می‌کند. برای تست رابط ساخته شده، اما همان کنترل برای خواندن صفحهٔ عمومی بعد از رندر هم به‌کار می‌رود: باز کردن URL مجاز، صبر تا عنصر مشخص ظاهر شود، و برداشتن متن قیمت یا عنوان از DOM. این با کرالر لینک‌یاب فرق دارد. کشف URL را در کرالر چیست جدا نگه دارید؛ اینجا رندر است نه خزیدن بی‌پایان. ابزار تست را با مجوز برداشت قاطی نکنید. اینکه بتوانید صفحه را در مرورگر خودتان باز کنید، به‌معنی اجازهٔ استخراج انبوه نیست. robots.txt، شرایط استفاده و نوع داده همچنان اول می‌آیند. این مقاله روش ورود به ناحیهٔ قفل، حل کپچا یا پنهان‌کردن ربات را آموزش نمی‌دهد. اگر بدون آن‌ها داده در دسترس نیست، منبع را از محدوده حذف کنید یا خوراک رسمی بخواهید. خروجی باید همان فیلد توافق‌شده باشد: عنوان، قیمت عددی، URL، زمان برداشت. اسکرین شات زیبا داده نیست. اگر بعد از رندر هنوز فیلد در DOM نیست — مثلاً داخل تصویر یا بوم — Playwright معجزه نمی‌کند. آن محدودیت را قبل از برآورد بنویسید. چه مسیری برای چه صفحه آنچه در پاسخ HTTP می‌بینید مسیر اول چرا عنوان و قیمت داخل HTML درخواست معمولی ارزان‌تر و پایدارتر JSON داخل اسکریپت صفحه پارس همان پاسخ مرورگر چیزی اضافه نمی‌کند کارت‌ها فقط بعد از اجرای JS رندر انتخابی DOM همان منبع است فیلد فقط در API رسمی قرارداد API اسکرپ صفحه اتلاف است کی HTML کافی نیست؟ فروشگاه‌های مدرن اغلب فهرست کالا را با جاوااسکریپت می‌سازند. درخواست ساده یک پوسته خالی برمی‌گرداند. اگر در ابزار توسعه‌دهنده، بعد از بارگذاری، کارت‌ها در DOM هستند، رندر معنا دارد. اگر همان داده در درخواست شبکه به‌صورت JSON عمومی می‌آید، همان JSON را با قرارداد و نرخ محترمانه بخوانید؛ روشن‌کردن مرورگر هزینهٔ اضافه است. اول پاسخ خام را ببینید؛ بعد تصمیم بگیرید مرورگر لازم است یا نه. صفحهٔ فیلتر که نتایج را بدون بارگذاری مجدد عوض می‌کند همین الگو را دارد. صرافی که جدول نرخ را سمت کلاینت به‌روز می‌کند هم ممکن است HTML اولیه را خالی بگذارد؛ معماری ویترین را در طراحی سایت صرافی جدا ببینید و اسکرپ را با دورزدن احراز قاطی نکنید. گردشگری که تور را با فیلتر تاریخ می‌آورد اگر ترکیب را در HTML ندهد، رندر یا API رسمی مطرح می‌شود — سیاست URL را در سئو سایت گردشگری بخوانید نه به‌عنوان دستور خزیدن فیلتر بی‌پایان. قانون عملی: یک URL نمونه را با درخواست ساده و با مرورگر مقایسه کنید. اگر فیلد در هر دو یکی است، مرورگر را برای تولید روشن نکنید. اگر فقط در مرورگر هست، همان درخواست‌ها را در محدودهٔ مجاز و با تأخیر اجرا کنید. حجم را از نمونه بسنجید؛ «همهٔ سایت» برآورد نیست. تفاوت Playwright با Scrapy و Selenium چیست؟ Scrapy زمان‌بند، صف و خط لولهٔ آیتم است و پیش‌فرض مرورگر باز نمی‌کند. برای HTML ایستا سریع و کم‌هزینه است. Playwright مرورگر واقعی است: حافظه، CPU و نسخهٔ مرورگر می‌خواهد. یکی جایگزین دیگری نیست. تیم بالغ HTML را با زمان‌بند HTTP می‌گیرد و فقط URLهایی را که واقعاً به DOM نیاز دارند به رندر می‌سپارد. Selenium هم مرورگر را کنترل می‌کند، معمولاً با لایهٔ درایور جدا. Playwright مرورگر را همراه نصب می‌کند و انتظار برای ظاهر شدن عنصر در APIاش جاافتاده‌تر است. انتخاب ابزار تست موجود تیم را به اسکرپ تولید تبدیل نکنید. اگر سوئیت سلنیوم دارید، مهاجرت اجباری نیست؛ هزینهٔ نگهداری دو مسیر را بسنجید. این صفحه آموزش نصب حمله نیست — فقط مرز نقش است. ادغام Scrapy با رندر انتخابی در پروژه‌های بزرگ رایج است: کشف و تکرار روی HTTP، رندر فقط برای برگه‌هایی که نمونه ثابت کرده DOM لازم دارند. اگر همهٔ درخواست‌ها را به مرورگر بدهید، هزینه خطی با تعداد URL بالا می‌رود و یک تغییر قالب همه را می‌خواباند. پایداری سلکتور را چطور نگه داریم؟ کلاس CSS تصادفی با اولین بازطراحی می‌میرد. سلکتور پایدار به نقش و متن مرئی نزدیک‌تر است: برچسب «قیمت»، ویژگی دسترس‌پذیری، یا ساختار تکرارشوندهٔ کارت — نه div.sc-a1b2 . بعد از هر اجرا، تعداد کارت و نوع فیلد را چک کنید. اگر صفر شد، اجرا بایستد نه اینکه قیمت خالی را حقیقت فرض کند. به نقش عنصر بچسبید، نه به کلاس تولیدشدهٔ باندلر. صبر را به زمان ثابت گره نزنید. «سه ثانیه sleep» در شبکهٔ کند دروغ می‌گوید و در شبکهٔ سریع پول می‌سوزاند. صبر تا سلکتور مشخص یا تا درخواست دادهٔ همان صفحه تمام شود دقیق‌تر است. متن فارسی طول برچسب را عوض می‌کند؛ نمونه را با عنوان واقعی بسنجید نه با lorem. برای کاتالوگ کالا، شناسه را از URL پایدار یا SKU روی صفحه بگیرید نه از ترتیب کارت. تطبیق را در استخراج داده محصول جدا بنویسید تا این مقاله روی رندر بماند. پایش قیمت هم به همان سلکتور شکننده حساس است؛ هشدار تغییر را در مانیتورینگ قیمت رقبا ببینید. هزینه اجرا از کجا می‌آید؟ هر نمونهٔ مرورگر RAM و CPU می‌گیرد. موازی‌سازی بی‌رویه سرور شما را می‌کشد و منبع مقصد را هم تحت فشار می‌گذارد. نرخ محترمانه بخشی از کیفیت است نه ضعف. مرورگر را بین درخواست‌های همان دامنه بی‌خودی از نو روشن نکنید؛ و صفحه را بعد از خواندن ببندید تا نشت حافظه نسازد. هزینهٔ پنهان، تعمیر است. قالب فصلی، بنر و تست A/B سلکتور را می‌شکند. اگر بودجه فقط برای اسکریپت اول است، رندر پایدار قول ندهید. گاهی API ناقص با سه فیلد، از مرورگر کامل با ده فیلد شکننده صادقانه‌تر است. برآورد را با ساعت رندر و ساعت نگهداری بنویسید، نه با «یک بار می‌نویسیم تمام». اشتباهات رایج اسکرپ با Playwright روشن‌کردن مرورگر قبل از دیدن HTML خام چسبیدن به کلاس فشرده‌شده sleep ثابت به‌جای انتظار عنصر موازی‌سازی تا حد اختلال منبع فرض اینکه ابزار تست مجوز برداشت می‌دهد نادیده‌گرفتن robots و نوع داده تحویل بدون زمان برداشت و بدون گزارش شکست چک‌لیست قبل از رندر مرورگر HTML خام و تب شبکه را با یک URL نمونه مقایسه کرده‌اید. API یا JSON داخل صفحه را رد نکرده‌اید. مسیرهای Disallow و دادهٔ شخصی از محدوده خارج‌اند. سلکتور به نقش یا متن پایدار وصل است. توقف خودکار وقتی تعداد کارت صفر است تعریف شده. تأخیر بین درخواست‌ها با حجم واقعی می‌خواند. زمان برداشت و نسخهٔ انتخاب در خروجی هست. بودجهٔ نگهداری قالب در برآورد آمده است. جمع‌بندی: رندر انتخابی، نه مرورگر برای همه اسکرپ با Playwright یعنی خواندن DOM بعد از جاوااسکریپت، وقتی HTML کافی نیست. Scrapy زمان‌بند است؛ Selenium مسیر دیگر کنترل مرورگر است. سلکتور پایدار و هزینهٔ اجرا تصمیم را واقعی می‌کنند. رتبه، پوشش نامحدود و دورزدن قفل در کار نیست. اگر می‌خواهید محدودهٔ رندر را روی منبع مجاز خودتان تعریف کنید، از صفحه اسکرپ داده روبینش و فرم مشاوره شروع کنید. این مقاله تعرفه نمی‌سازد. یک URL نمونه با دو مسیر — HTTP و مرورگر — این هفته، از روشن‌کردن کرومیوم برای تمام سایت مفیدتر است.

title: A record label told as a science-fiction story
author: Spicanet
summary: Most label sites are a list of releases with cover art and buy links. That's fine. It's also forgettable. Universal Rift Records is an independent electronic music label where high-velocity drum & bass, hypnotic trance and mechanical techno converge, and the catalogue isn't just a list. It's a science-fiction world told in chapters, from first contact to the awakening of a machine supermind. The site is live, and this is how I think about building a label as a story. Why a story at all Electronic music already lives in sci-fi territory. The sounds, the titles, the artwork all lean toward space, machines and signals from somewhere else. Most labels gesture at that and move on. I wanted to commit to it: one world, one long arc, and every release a piece of it. That gives the catalogue a shape. A release isn't just the next one in the list. It's the next chapter, and it belongs somewhere. The sounds of one world Sound What it brings Drum & bass Velocity Trance Hypnosis Techno Machinery The territories The world is split into territories: Rift, Event Horizon, Starbirth and Signal. They give releases a place to belong, so a listener can follow a part of the world they like instead of scrolling a flat release list. I'm deliberately not spelling out every rule of each territory here. Some of that is for the music to do. Chapters, not just releases The story runs from first contact to the awakening of a machine supermind. Releases such as First Signal and Monolith sit inside that arc. The titles do some of the storytelling on their own, which is the point: you should be able to read the catalogue and feel the story moving even before you press play. The sounds meet in this world. Drum & bass brings the velocity. Trance brings the hypnosis. Techno brings the machinery. They aren't kept in separate rooms; the territories are where they meet. A catalogue should read like a story even before you press play. â€” the idea behind the label What the site holds The site is the label's home base. It holds the catalogue, the artist roster, a video archive and a demo submission form. Nothing exotic, but each piece is shaped by the world: the catalogue reads as chapters, and the territories give each release a place. Catalogue Artist roster Video archive Demo submissions The first release The inaugural release is by Nocterion, and it's out on Bandcamp and the major streaming services. The label site doesn't try to replace those. It points at them, the same way a book's website points at where to buy the book. Sending a demo. If you make drum & bass, trance or techno that sounds like it belongs in this world, there's a demo submission form on the site. Read a bit of the story first. It helps. What I ask of every new release Does it move the story forward or deepen a part of it? Which territory does it belong to? Do the title and artwork read as part of the same world? Will it sit comfortably next to First Signal and Monolith? Is it out where people actually listen? What's honestly early The label is young. With an inaugural release, the catalogue is at the beginning of its story, not the middle. That's how labels start, and I'd rather say so than dress it up with borrowed credibility. The story is also a commitment. Once you tell people a world has rules, you have to keep them. Every future release has to fit, which is harder than just putting out the next good track. If you're building a label site Give the catalogue a shape and not just a list Link out to where people actually listen and buy Keep a video archive in one place Make demo submission easy to find Don't invent history the label doesn't have Note: How it's built. In general terms: a content site with a structured catalogue of releases, artists and videos, each release tied to a place in the story, and outbound links to Bandcamp and streaming services for listening. Have a listen Universal Rift Records lives at universalrift.com . My other projects are on spicanet.net/products . Originally published on spicanet.dev .

title: From Manual Processes to Software: How Systems Analysis and Design Solve Business Problems
author: Vincent Tommi
summary: Imagine a university where students wait in long queues to register for courses, lecturers submit examination marks on paper, and students wait weeks to receive their transcripts. These problems may appear to be caused by slow administrative processes. However, the underlying issue could be a system that relies on manual work, disconnected records, and repetitive tasks. As developers, we should not rush to write code before understanding the problem. This is where systems analysis and design become important. In this article, we will explore how a university can move from manual academic processes to a computer-based information system. 1. Understanding Systems, Systems Analysis, and Systems Design Before building a solution, we need to understand three fundamental concepts. What is a system? A system is a collection of interconnected components that work together to achieve a common goal. In a university, the academic administration system consists of: People: Students, lecturers, registrars, and examination officers. Processes: Student registration, examination marking, and transcript generation. Data: Student details, course registrations, examination marks, and academic records. Technology: Computers, databases, networks, and software applications. These components work together to support academic administration. From a developer's perspective, this means that a university information system is more than a collection of web pages. It is a combination of people, processes, data, and technology. What is systems analysis? Systems analysis is the process of examining an existing system to understand how it works, identify its problems, and determine what users need from a new or improved solution. For example, before developing a transcript-generation application, we might investigate: How examination marks are currently submitted. Who verifies and approves the marks. How grades are calculated. Why transcript requests take so long. What information must appear on a transcript. This investigation helps us define the actual problem instead of making assumptions. What is systems design? Systems design translates the requirements identified during analysis into a technical plan for the proposed solution. For the university, this could involve designing: Database tables and relationships. User interfaces for students and lecturers. APIs for submitting and retrieving examination marks. Authentication and role-based authorization. Grade calculation and transcript-generation processes. Reports and audit logs. For example, a developer might use Django REST Framework to build an API, PostgreSQL to store academic records, and React to build the user interface. The important distinction is that analysis determines what the system needs to achieve, while design determines how the system will achieve it. 2. Three Problems with the Manual System and Their Solutions Let's examine three practical problems and how software can address them. Problem 1: Slow student registration When students register using paper forms, university staff must manually review documents, enter details, and update records. This can create long queues, duplicate records, and delays in confirming registration. The software solution An online student registration system could allow students to submit their details electronically. The system could: Validate required fields. Check whether a student already exists. Verify course prerequisites where applicable. Store registration details in a centralized database. Generate registration confirmations automatically. For example, a Django backend could expose a registration API that validates submitted data before saving it to PostgreSQL. Instead of repeatedly entering information from paper forms, staff could retrieve records from the database. Problem 2: Errors when recording examination marks Manual mark entry introduces opportunities for transcription errors, incorrect calculations, and misplaced documents. For example, a lecturer might record a mark of 76 on a paper sheet, but someone entering the result into a spreadsheet could accidentally enter 67. Such mistakes can affect a student's final grade and academic progress. The software solution A computer-based examination management system could provide: Validated mark-entry forms. Student and course identification checks. Automatic grade calculations based on approved grading rules. Audit logs showing who changed a mark and when. Approval workflows before results are published. For instance, the backend could reject marks outside the permitted range, provided the institution's grading rules define that range. However, validation alone is not enough. The system must also support verification and controlled correction of marks. Problem 3: Delayed transcript generation When transcripts are prepared manually, examination officers may need to collect marks from several documents, calculate grades, verify results, and type the final report. This takes time, especially when many students request transcripts simultaneously. The software solution A transcript-generation module could retrieve approved academic records from the database and produce a transcript automatically. The workflow might look like this: The examination officer approves the student's results. The system retrieves the student's courses and approved marks. The system calculates grades according to university rules. The system generates the transcript. An authorized officer verifies or approves it before release, where required. Automation can reduce repetitive work, but the system must preserve accuracy, privacy, and the university's approval procedures. 3. Identifying and Consulting Key Stakeholders A technically sound application can still fail if it does not address the needs of its users. That is why systems analysts consult stakeholders during the analysis phase. The university project would involve several groups. Stakeholder Information to collect Students Registration challenges, transcript requests, and access requirements Lecturers Mark submission procedures, grading rules, and correction processes Examination officers Result verification, grade approval, and transcript preparation Registry staff Student records, registration workflows, and document requirements ICT staff Existing infrastructure, integrations, security, and technical constraints University management Budget, institutional policies, reporting requirements, and project goals How would we collect this information? As a systems analyst, I would use several techniques. Interviews: Speak directly with examination officers, lecturers, and registry staff to understand their daily challenges. Observation: Watch how student registration and transcript preparation currently work. Questionnaires: Collect feedback from a larger number of students and staff. Document analysis: Review existing registration forms, mark sheets, transcript templates, and academic policies. The information gathered would help us produce clear system requirements before development begins. 4. Why Analyze the Existing System Before Designing a New One? One of the biggest mistakes in software development is building a solution before understanding the problem. Suppose the university's results are delayed because examination officers must obtain approvals from several departments. Developing software that only calculates grades faster will not necessarily solve the main problem. The approval process itself may need improvement. Analyzing the existing system helps us: Identify root causes. We can distinguish between problems caused by manual data entry, inefficient workflows, missing approvals, and technical limitations. Avoid unnecessary costs. Understanding requirements early reduces the likelihood of building features that users do not need. Improve user adoption. Consulting stakeholders helps ensure that the new system supports their actual responsibilities. Reduce implementation risks. Early analysis can reveal data migration challenges, security requirements, and integration issues. Establish measurable goals. The university can compare performance before and after implementation. For example, it could measure average registration completion time, the number of mark-entry errors, and the time required to issue approved transcripts. These measurements help determine whether the new system is delivering meaningful improvements. 5. Connecting Systems Analysis and Design to the Software Development Life Cycle Systems analysis and design are also closely connected to the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). A simplified development process could look like this: Planning: Define the problem, objectives, scope, and available resources. Analysis: Investigate current processes and gather user requirements. Design: Plan the database, architecture, interfaces, security, and workflows. Implementation: Develop the application and integrate its components. Testing: Verify functionality, accuracy, security, and performance. Deployment: Introduce the system to the university and train users. Maintenance: Fix defects, monitor performance, and improve the system over time. These stages help organize development, although real projects may revisit earlier stages when new requirements or problems emerge. Conclusion Moving a university from manual administration to a computer-based information system involves more than digitizing paper records. The real goal is to understand existing challenges, identify what stakeholders need, and design a solution that improves how the institution operates. Systems analysis helps us understand the problem. Systems design provides a blueprint for solving it. Software development then turns that blueprint into a working solution. As developers, we should remember that writing code is only one part of solving a business problem. The quality of the final solution depends heavily on how well we understand the people, processes, and requirements behind it. A question for fellow developers: Have you ever worked on a project where the technical solution was straightforward, but understanding the business process was the real challenge? What did you learn from that experience?

title: Daytona surpasses $1 billion valuation
author: Hacks.gr
summary: Daytona has raised a $60 million Series B round led by FirstMark Growth, pushing its valuation to $1 billion. The three-year-old startup provides isolated developer environments running on Linux, Windows, macOS, and GPUs, tailored specifically for long-running AI workloads. The funding round was led by FirstMark Growth, bringing the total funding Daytona has raised since its founding three years ago to $91 million. The investment teams of Qualcomm, Samsung, and Okta also participated. The company is headquartered in New York. Founder and CEO is Ivan Burazin, while the leadership team also includes architect Goran Draganic and technical director Vedran Jukic.
